title: Semiconductor physics for engineers: doping, p-n junctions
text:
CHAPTER 5. THE TRANSISTOR
SECTION 5.1. SEMICONDUCTOR PHYSICS FOR ENGINEERS: DOPING, P-N JUNCTIONS

Vacuum tubes switched fast but were hot, large, fragile and power-hungry. The device that replaced them, the transistor, does the same job inside a solid crystal, with no heater and no vacuum. To understand how a transistor switches (Sections 5.2 and 5.3) and why it could be shrunk by a factor of millions (Chapter 6), you need a working model of semiconductors. This section gives that model: energy bands, electrons and holes, doping, and the p-n junction diode, with the key equations an engineer uses.

1. Conductors, insulators and semiconductors

In a solid, the allowed energies of electrons form bands separated by forbidden gaps. Two bands matter:

  - the valence band, the highest band that is filled with electrons at absolute zero; electrons here are bound in chemical bonds;
  - the conduction band, the next band up; electrons here are free to move through the crystal and carry current.

The band gap Eg is the energy between the top of the valence band and the bottom of the conduction band.

  Metals: bands overlap or are partly filled, so there are always free electrons. Conduct well.
  Insulators: large gap (for example about 9 eV for silicon dioxide), so essentially no electrons reach the conduction band at room temperature.
  Semiconductors: moderate gap, such as about 1.12 eV for silicon and about 0.66 eV for germanium at room temperature, so a few electrons are thermally excited across the gap.

Thermal energy at room temperature is about kT = 0.0259 eV (at 300 K), much smaller than the gap, so excitation across the gap is rare but not negligible, and it rises very steeply with temperature, roughly as exp(-Eg / (2kT)).

2. Electrons and holes

When an electron in pure silicon is excited into the conduction band, it leaves behind an empty state in a bond: a hole. A neighboring bound electron can move into that hole, which moves the hole the other way. The result behaves exactly like a positive charge carrier moving through the crystal. So a semiconductor has two kinds of carrier:

    electrons (negative), concentration n, in the conduction band
    holes (positive), concentration p, in the valence band

In a pure ("intrinsic") semiconductor, electrons and holes are created in pairs, so n = p = ni, the intrinsic carrier concentration. For silicon at 300 K, ni is about 1 * 10^10 per cubic centimeter. Silicon has about 5 * 10^22 atoms per cubic centimeter, so only about one atom in 10^12 contributes a carrier. Pure silicon is a poor conductor.

A fundamental relation (the law of mass action) holds in thermal equilibrium, whether the material is pure or doped:

    n * p = ni^2

3. Doping

The magic of semiconductors is that their conductivity can be controlled precisely, over many orders of magnitude, by adding tiny amounts of impurity atoms.

Silicon is in group IV of the periodic table: each atom has four valence electrons and forms four bonds in the diamond crystal lattice.

  n-type doping: add a group V element (phosphorus, arsenic, antimony), which has five valence electrons. Four form bonds; the fifth is very loosely bound (about 0.05 eV) and at room temperature is almost always freed into the conduction band. The impurity is called a donor. With donor concentration Nd much greater than ni:

      n is approximately Nd,   p = ni^2 / Nd

  p-type doping: add a group III element (boron, aluminum, gallium), which has three valence electrons. One bond is missing an electron, creating a hole that is easily freed. The impurity is an acceptor. With acceptor concentration Na:

      p is approximately Na,   n = ni^2 / Na

Worked example. Dope silicon with Nd = 10^16 phosphorus atoms per cubic centimeter (about one impurity per 5 million silicon atoms). Then n is about 10^16 and p = (10^10)^2 / 10^16 = 10^4 per cubic centimeter. Electrons are the majority carriers, outnumbering holes by a factor of 10^12; holes are the minority carriers. The conductivity has increased by about a million times over pure silicon.

Conductivity is:

    sigma = q * (n * mu_n + p * mu_p)

where q is the electron charge (1.6 * 10^-19 C) and mu_n, mu_p are the electron and hole mobilities (in silicon, roughly 1,400 and 450 cm^2/(V s) at low doping). Electrons are more mobile than holes, which is why n-type devices tend to be faster and why, in CMOS (Section 5.3), the p-type transistors are usually made wider than the n-type ones.

The extreme sensitivity to impurities has an engineering consequence: semiconductor devices require extraordinarily pure starting material. Purities of better than 99.9999999 percent ("nine nines") became standard for silicon, achieved by methods such as zone refining (developed at Bell Labs by William Pfann in the early 1950s) and later chemical purification. Single crystals are grown by the Czochralski method, pulling a seed crystal slowly out of molten silicon.

4. Drift and diffusion

Carriers move by two mechanisms:

  Drift: in an electric field E, carriers acquire an average velocity v = mu * E. Electron current density from drift is q * n * mu_n * E.

  Diffusion: carriers spread from regions of high concentration to low, like ink in water. The diffusion current density for electrons is q * Dn * dn/dx, where Dn is the diffusion coefficient.

Mobility and diffusion are linked by the Einstein relation:

    D / mu = kT / q   (about 25.9 mV at 300 K)

The quantity kT/q, the thermal voltage VT, appears everywhere in semiconductor equations.

5. The p-n junction

Now put p-type and n-type silicon in contact within one crystal. (In practice the junction is formed by doping different regions of a single crystal, not by pressing two pieces together.)

Formation of the depletion region. At the boundary there are many electrons on the n side and many holes on the p side. Electrons diffuse into the p side and holes into the n side, where they recombine. This leaves behind a thin region near the junction with no free carriers, called the depletion region, containing only the fixed ionized impurity atoms: positive donor ions on the n side, negative acceptor ions on the p side. These fixed charges create an electric field pointing from n to p, which opposes further diffusion. Equilibrium is reached when drift caused by this field exactly balances diffusion.

The built-in potential across the junction is:

    Vbi = VT * ln( Na * Nd / ni^2 )

Example: Na = Nd = 10^16 per cubic centimeter. Vbi = 0.0259 * ln(10^32 / 10^20) = 0.0259 * ln(10^12) = 0.0259 * 27.6, about 0.72 V.

You cannot measure this voltage with a voltmeter (contact potentials at the metal connections cancel it), but it controls how the junction behaves under bias.

Forward bias. Apply a positive voltage V to the p side relative to the n side. This opposes the built-in potential, lowering the barrier. The number of carriers able to diffuse across rises exponentially with V, and a large current flows.

Reverse bias. Apply negative V to the p side. The barrier increases, the depletion region widens, and only a tiny leakage current flows, carried by the few minority carriers thermally generated near the junction.

6. The diode equation

The current through an ideal p-n junction is given by the Shockley diode equation (William Shockley, 1949):

    I = Is * ( exp( V / (n * VT) ) - 1 )

where Is is the saturation current (very small, perhaps 10^-14 A for a small silicon diode), VT is the thermal voltage, and n is an ideality factor between 1 and 2.

What the equation says:

  - For forward bias of a few tenths of a volt, the exponential dominates. With n = 1, every increase of VT * ln(10), about 60 mV, multiplies the current by ten. That is why a silicon diode seems to "turn on" at about 0.6 to 0.7 V: below that the current is negligible, above it the current rises extremely steeply.
  - For reverse bias, I is approximately -Is, tiny.
  - Is depends strongly on temperature, roughly doubling for every few degrees of increase; for a fixed current, the forward voltage of a silicon diode falls by about 2 mV per degree Celsius. (This is used in temperature sensors, and it is a reason for careful thermal design in power electronics.)

Junction capacitance. The depletion region is an insulating layer between two conducting regions, so it acts as a capacitor whose capacitance decreases as reverse bias widens it. This capacitance must be charged and discharged when a junction switches, which limits switching speed, the same RC limit as in tubes (Section 4.1), now at a much smaller scale. Shrinking devices shrinks this capacitance, one reason smaller transistors are faster (Section 6.2).

Breakdown. At large reverse voltages the field becomes strong enough to cause avalanche multiplication or quantum tunneling (Zener effect), and current rises sharply. Zener diodes exploit this as voltage references.

7. A brief history

Semiconductor effects were known long before anyone understood them.

  - In 1874 Karl Ferdinand Braun observed that contacts between metal points and certain crystals conducted current better in one direction than the other: rectification.
  - In the early 1900s, radio receivers used crystal detectors ("cat's whiskers"): a fine wire touching a crystal of galena (lead sulfide) or silicon. Greenleaf Whittier Pickard patented a silicon detector in 1906. Crystal detectors were finicky, and vacuum tubes largely displaced them in the 1920s.
  - The quantum theory of solids developed in the late 1920s and 1930s (Felix Bloch, Alan Wilson and others) explained band structure and why semiconductors behave as they do.
  - During World War II, microwave radar needed detectors faster than tubes could provide, which revived crystal diodes. Intensive research on purifying germanium and silicon, at Bell Labs, at Purdue University, at MIT's Radiation Laboratory and elsewhere, produced much better materials and understanding.
  - In 1939-1940 Russell Ohl at Bell Labs, studying silicon samples, discovered that some contained a boundary between regions of different impurity types, which produced a voltage when illuminated: the p-n junction (and an early silicon photovoltaic cell). The terms "p-type" and "n-type" came from this work.

By 1945 Bell Labs had the materials knowledge, the theoretical understanding and the motivation (replacing unreliable tubes and mechanical relays in the telephone network) to try to make a solid-state amplifier. That effort, Section 5.2, produced the transistor in 1947.

8. Why this matters for a mechatronics engineer

The p-n junction is the building block of almost every electronic device you will use:

  - rectifier diodes in power supplies and motor drives;
  - flyback diodes across relay and solenoid coils, which absorb the inductive voltage spike when the coil is switched off (Section 2.1's relays still need this);
  - LEDs (junctions in materials whose band gap emits visible or infrared light) and photodiodes (junctions that generate current from light), used in optical encoders and sensors;
  - solar cells;
  - bipolar transistors (two junctions) and the source/drain junctions of MOSFETs.

And it underlies the computing hardware that runs AI: a modern GPU contains tens of billions of transistors, each defined by doped regions and junctions in silicon, the same physics as in this section.

9. Summary

  - Semiconductors have a moderate band gap (Si about 1.12 eV, Ge about 0.66 eV); carriers are electrons in the conduction band and holes in the valence band, with n * p = ni^2 and ni about 10^10 per cubic centimeter for Si at 300 K.
  - Donors (group V) make n-type material; acceptors (group III) make p-type; tiny concentrations change conductivity by many orders of magnitude.
  - Carriers move by drift (mu * E) and diffusion (D * gradient), with D / mu = kT/q.
  - A p-n junction forms a depletion region and built-in potential Vbi = VT ln(Na Nd / ni^2), about 0.7 V for typical doping.
  - The Shockley equation I = Is (exp(V / (n VT)) - 1) describes rectification: about 60 mV per decade of current.
  - Semiconductor effects were exploited in crystal radio detectors from the early 1900s; wartime radar research and Ohl's 1939-1940 discovery of the p-n junction prepared the way for the transistor.
